claim: The Ca2+-activated TMEM16 family of membrane proteins plays an important role in collapsing asymmetric lipid distribution by spontaneously and bidirectionally scrambling phospholipids between the two leaflets.
source: The Ca 2+ -activated TMEM16 family of membrane proteins plays an important role in collapsing this asymmetric lipid distribution by spontaneously and bidirectionally scrambling phospholipids between the two leaflets
evidence: This is a general statement about TMEM16 function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Lipid scrambling by TMEM16 can occur via an open hydrophilic pathway (groove) that spans the membrane.
source: While evidence shows that lipid scrambling can occur via an open hydrophilic pathway (groove) that spans the membrane
evidence: This statement references existing evidence from the field, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Over 700 scrambling events were captured in aggregate across 27 structures from five different TMEM16 family members.
source: we captured over 700 scrambling events in aggregate
evidence: This is a direct quantitative result from the computational simulations performed in this study.

claim: All TMEM16 structures thin the membrane.
source: We show that all TMEM16 structures thin the membrane
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data presented in the manuscript, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of scrambling (>90%) occurs at the groove only when TM4 and TM6 have sufficiently separated.
source: the majority of scrambling (>90%) occurs at the groove only when TM4 and TM6 have sufficiently separated
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data, supported by Table 1 showing 92% of events occur in-the-groove.

claim: 60 scrambling events occurred outside the canonical groove, over 90% of which took place at the dimer–dimer interface in mammalian TMEM16s.
source: we also observed 60 scrambling events that occurred outside the canonical groove, over 90% of which took place at the dimer–dimer interface in mammalian TMEM16s
evidence: This is a direct quantitative result from the simulations, supported by Table 1 and Figure 4.

claim: The TMEM16 family includes lipid scramblases, ion channels, and members that can facilitate both lipid and ion permeation.
source: The TMEM16 family of eukaryotic membrane proteins, also known as anoctamins, is comprised of lipid scramblases (Suzuki et al., 2013; Di Zanni et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2018), ion channels (Yang et al., 2008; Caputo et al., 2008; Stöhr et al., 2009; Schroeder et al., 2008), and members that can facilitate both lipid and ion permeation
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: All characterized TMEM16s require Ca2+ to achieve their maximum transport activity.
source: So far, all characterized TMEM16s require Ca2+ to achieve their maximum transport activity, whether that be passive ion movement or lipid flow down their electrochemical gradients
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: TMEM16s play critical roles in blood coagulation, bone mineralization, mucus secretion, smooth muscle contraction, and membrane fusion.
source: TMEM16s play critical roles in a variety of physiological processes including blood coagulation (Yang et al., 2012; Castoldi et al., 2011; Boisseau et al., 2018; Brooks et al., 2015), bone mineralization (Tsutsumi et al., 2004), mucus secretion (Cabrita et al., 2021), smooth muscle contraction (Huang et al., 2012), and membrane fusion (Griffin et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies demonstrating these physiological roles.

claim: Mutations of TMEM16 have been implicated in several cancers, neuronal disorder SCAR10, and SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Mutations of TMEM16 have also been implicated in several cancers (Mohsenzadegan et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2021; Cereda et al., 2010), neuronal disorder SCAR10 (Vermeer et al., 2010; Petkovic et al., 2019), and SARS-CoV-2 infection (Braga et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies linking TMEM16 mutations to disease.

claim: 63 experimental structures of TMEM16s have been determined over 10 years.
source: Over the 10 years, 63 experimental structures of TMEM16s have been determined
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of solved structures, supported by knowledge of the structural biology literature.

claim: All TMEM16 structures except one fungal Aspergillus fumigatus TMEM16 monomer are homodimers with a butterfly-like fold.
source: All structures, except for one of fungal Aspergillus fumigatus TMEM16 (afTMEM16) (Falzone et al., 2022), which is a monomer, are homodimers with a butterfly-like fold
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Each TMEM16 subunit is comprised of 10 transmembrane (TM) helices with the final helix (TM10) forming most of the dimer interface.
source: each subunit is comprised of 10 transmembrane (TM) helices with the final helix (TM10) forming most of the dimer interface
evidence: This is a structural description supported by citations to experimental structures.

claim: Residues on TM6 form half of a highly conserved Ca2+-binding site that accommodates up to two ions.
source: Residues on TM6 form half of a highly conserved Ca2+-binding site that accommodates up to two ions
evidence: This is a structural feature described in the literature and supported by experimental structures.

claim: TM6, along with TM3, TM4, and TM5, forms a membrane spanning groove that contains hydrophilic residues.
source: TM6, along with TM3, TM4, and TM5, also forms a membrane spanning groove that contains hydrophilic residues that are shielded from the hydrophobic core of the bilayer in Ca2+-free states
evidence: This is a structural description based on experimental structures.

claim: Ca2+ binding is associated with the movement of the upper portion of TM4 away from TM6 which effectively exposes (opens) the hydrophilic groove to the bilayer.
source: Ca2+ binding is also associated with the movement of the upper portion of TM4 away from TM6 which effectively exposes (opens) the hydrophilic groove to the bilayer
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by citations to experimental structures.

claim: Lipids can traverse the membrane bilayer by moving their headgroups along the water-filled hydrophilic groove while their tails project into the hydrophobic center of the bilayer, according to the 'credit card model'.
source: lipids can traverse the membrane bilayer by moving their headgroups along the water-filled hydrophilic groove (between TM4 and TM6) while their tails project into the hydrophobic center of the bilayer. This mechanism for scrambling, first proposed by Menon and Pomorski, is often referred to as the 'credit card model'
evidence: This mechanism is supported by prior theoretical work and MD simulations cited in the text.

claim: Lipids experience a relatively low energy barrier for scrambling in open nhTMEM16 (<1 kcal/mol compared to 20–50 kcal/mol directly through the bilayer).
source: Lipids experience a relatively low energy barrier for scrambling in open nhTMEM16 (<1 kcal/mol compared to 20–50 kcal/mol directly through the bilayer)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior simulation studies.

claim: Zwitterionic lipid headgroups stack in the open groove along their dipoles, which may help energetically stabilize them during scrambling.
source: Simulations also indicate that zwitterionic lipid headgroups stack in the open groove along their dipoles, which may help energetically stabilize them during scrambling
evidence: This is based on prior simulation observations and involves speculation about energetic stabilization.

claim: No more than 14 spontaneous scrambling events have been reported in the absence of an applied voltage from prior simulation studies.
source: in aggregate, we estimate that no more than 14 scrambling events have been reported in the absence of an applied voltage
evidence: This is an estimate based on reviewing prior literature cited in the text.

claim: Approximately 800 scrambling events in aggregate have been seen in coarse-grained MD simulations for nhTMEM16, TMEM16K, mutant TMEM16F (F518H), and TMEM16A.
source: Many more scrambling events (~800 in aggregate) have been seen in coarse-grained MD (CGMD) simulations for nhTMEM16 (Stansfeld et al., 2015), TMEM16K (Bushell et al., 2019), mutant TMEM16F (F518H), and even TMEM16A (Li et al., 2024)
evidence: This is based on citations to prior CGMD simulation studies.

claim: Wild-type TMEM16F structures have failed to show open grooves wide enough to accommodate lipids, despite structures being solved under activating conditions.
source: This question has been triggered in part by the failure to determine wild-type (WT) TMEM16F structures with open grooves wide enough to accommodate lipids, despite structures being solved under activating conditions
evidence: This is based on citations to experimental structural studies of TMEM16F.

claim: Scrambling can occur in the absence of Ca2+ when the groove is presumably closed.
source: Further uncertainty stems from data showing that scrambling can occur in the absence of Ca2+ when the groove is presumably closed
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: afTMEM16 can scramble PEGylated lipids, which are too large for even the open groove.
source: afTMEM16 can scramble PEGylated lipids, which are too large for even the open groove
evidence: This is an experimental finding cited from Malvezzi et al., 2018.

claim: The bilayer adjacent to TMEM16 proteins is distorted whether the groove is open or closed, as shown in cryo-EM nanodiscs, MD simulations, and continuum models.
source: the bilayer adjacent to the protein, whether the groove is open or closed, is distorted in cryo-EM in nanodiscs (Falzone et al., 2022; Arndt et al., 2022; Kalienkova et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2019), MD simulations (Bushell et al., 2019; Bethel and Grabe, 2016; Khelashvili et al., 2020), and continuum models (Bethel and Grabe, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and computational studies.

claim: The membrane distortion is characterized by local bending and thinning adjacent to the groove, estimated to be 50–60% thinner than bulk for some family members.
source: The hallmark of this distortion is local bending and thinning adjacent to the groove (estimated to be 50–60% thinner than bulk for some family members)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies that quantified membrane thinning.

claim: No AAMD or CGMD simulation has reported scrambling by any WT TMEM16 harboring a closed groove.
source: To date, no AAMD or CGMD simulation has reported scrambling by any WT TMEM16 harboring a closed groove
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on reviewing prior simulation studies.

claim: Ions permeate through the lipid headgroup-lined hydrophilic groove of TMEM16K and nhTMEM16 according to AAMD simulations.
source: AAMD simulations have shown that ions permeate through the lipid headgroup-lined hydrophilic groove of TMEM16K and nhTMEM16
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior AAMD simulation studies.

claim: CGMD was the first computational method to identify nhTMEM16 as a scramblase.
source: CGMD, which was the first computational method to identify nhTMEM16 as a scramblase (Stansfeld et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the Stansfeld et al. 2015 study.

claim: The simulated membrane distortions qualitatively match experimental densities and shapes produced from AAMD simulations and continuum membrane models.
source: The shapes of the membrane near the protein qualitatively match the experimental densities and the shapes produced from AAMD simulations and continuum membrane models
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results in this study and prior work, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CG simulations capture the sinusoidal curve around both fungal scramblases in apo and Ca2+-bound states.
source: the CG simulations capture the sinusoidal curve around both fungal scramblases in apo and Ca2+-bound states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The membrane is flatter around TMEM16K and TMEM16F compared to the fungal members in both the nanodisc density and CGMD.
source: the membrane is flatter around TMEM16K and TMEM16F compared to the fungal members in both the nanodisc density and CGMD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results and experimental nanodisc densities, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Open-groove structures typically have an average of 2–3 lipids in the TM4/TM6 groove at any given time.
source: Open-groove structures typically have an average of 2–3 lipids in the TM4/TM6 groove at any given time (see Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data provided in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: All of the grooves are filled with water.
source: Additional analysis shows that all of the grooves are filled with water (Appendix 1—figure 2)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The open Ca2+-bound fungal nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) was the strongest scrambler with 24.4 ± 5.2 events per μs.
source: The strongest scrambler was the open-groove, Ca2+-bound fungal nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS), with 24.4 ± 5.2 events per μs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The open Ca2+-free nhTMEM16 structure (PDB ID 6QM6) scrambled lipids at 15.7 ± 3.9 events per μs.
source: the open Ca2+-free structure (PDB ID 6QM6), which is structurally very similar to PDB ID 4WIS, also scrambled lipids (15.7 ± 3.9 events per μs, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No scrambling events were observed for the intermediate- (PDB ID 6QMA) and closed- (PDB ID 6QM4, PDB ID 6QMB) groove nhTMEM16 structures.
source: we observed no scrambling events for the intermediate- (PDB ID 6QMA) and closed- (PDB ID 6QM4, PDB ID 6QMB) groove nhTMEM16 structures
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data.

claim: The open Ca2+-bound afTMEM16 cryo-EM structure (PDB ID 7RXG) is scrambling competent with 10.7 ± 2.9 events per μs.
source: our simulations identified the open Ca2+-bound cryo-EM structure (PDB ID 7RXG) as scrambling competent (10.7 ± 2.9 events per μs, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The Ca2+-free closed-groove afTMEM16 structure (PDB ID 7RXB) was not scrambling competent.
source: while the Ca2+-free closed-groove structure (PDB ID 7RXB) was not
evidence: This is a result from the simulation data.

claim: The Ca2+-bound TMEM16K X-ray structure (PDB ID 5OC9) facilitates scrambling at 8.2 ± 2.9 events per μs.
source: our simulations showed that the Ca2+-bound X-ray structure (PDB ID 5OC9) facilitates scrambling (8.2 ± 2.9 events per μs)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data.

claim: There was a stark asymmetry in the number of scrambling events between the two TMEM16K monomers, with >80% of events happening via chain B.
source: we found a stark asymmetry in the number of scrambling events between the two monomers, with >80% of events happening via chain B (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Chain B of TMEM16K has a slightly wider ER lumen-facing entrance to the groove in the experimental starting structure (PDB ID 5OC9).
source: chain B has a slightly wider endoplasmic reticulum (ER) lumen-facing entrance to the groove in the experimental starting structure (PDB ID 5OC9, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Chain B of TMEM16K spontaneously opened its groove more than subunit A during the simulation (8.2 ± 1.3 Å compared to 5.8 ± 0.6 Å on average).
source: spontaneously opened its groove more than subunit A during the simulation (8.2 ± 1.3 Å compared to 5.8 ± 0.6 Å on average, Figure 3—figure supplement 6A)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6A.

claim: The closed-groove TMEM16K conformation (PDB ID 6R7X) showed very little scrambling activity (0.4 ± 0.7 events per μs).
source: The closed-groove TMEM16K conformation (PDB ID 6R7X) showed very little scrambling activity (0.4 ± 0.7 events per μs)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data.

claim: None of the WT TMEM16F structures solved to date have exhibited an open hydrophilic groove, even those determined under activating conditions.
source: Although TMEM16F is a known lipid scramblase found in the plasma membrane of platelets (Suzuki et al., 2010), none of the WT structures solved to date, even those determined under activating conditions, have exhibited an open hydrophilic groove
evidence: This is a statement about experimental structures supported by citations.

claim: Ten WT TMEM16F structures were simulated and observed little to no lipid scrambling in each case.
source: We simulated 10 of these proteins and observed little to no lipid scrambling in each case (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a result from the simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The F518H mutation turns TMEM16F into a constitutively active scramblase.
source: Others have shown that mutations at position F518 turn TMEM16F into a constitutively active scramblase (Le et al., 2019b)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J) was the only system initiated directly from a solved structure that showed scrambling activity (11.3 ± 1.6 events per μs).
source: TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J) was the only system initiated directly from a solved structure that showed scrambling activity (11.3 ± 1.6 events per μs, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: A WT TMEM16F with a single open groove obtained from AAMD (6QP6*) showed moderate lipid scrambling activity (3.0 ± 1.6 events per μs).
source: we performed CGMD on a WT TMEM16F with a single open groove obtained from AAMD initiated from a closed-state structure (cluster 10 in Khelashvili et al., 2022, 6QP6* in Figure 2A). We observed moderate lipid scrambling activity (3.0 ± 1.6 events per μs)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TMEM16A functions as an ion channel but lacks lipid scrambling activity.
source: we simulated six structures of mouse TMEM16A, which functions as an ion channel but lacks lipid scrambling activity (Paulino et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Both the Ca2+-bound (PDB ID 5OYB) and the Ca2+-free (PDB ID 5OYG) experimental TMEM16A structures failed to induce scrambling in the CGMD simulations.
source: As expected, both the Ca2+-bound (PDB ID 5OYB) and the Ca2+-free (PDB ID 5OYG) experimental structures failed to induce scrambling in the CGMD simulations
evidence: This is a result from the simulation data.

claim: A TMEM16A state with an open hydrophilic groove predicted by Jia and Chen (5OYB*) scrambled a single lipid through each groove.
source: However, a TMEM16A state with an open hydrophilic groove predicted by Jia and Chen (5OYB*, simulations initiated from PDB ID 5OYB; Jia and Chen, 2021) did scramble a single lipid through each groove
evidence: This is a result from the simulation data.

claim: 92% of the observed scrambling events occur along TM4 and TM6 with headgroups embedded in the open hydrated groove, in line with the credit card model.
source: In our CGMD simulations, 92% of the observed scrambling events occur along TM4 and TM6 with headgroups embedded in the open hydrated groove, in line with the credit card model, which we refer to as 'in-the-groove' scrambling (Table 1)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation data shown in Table 1.

claim: All the TMEM16 structures included in this study thin the membrane to 23 Å or less, which is at least 7 Å thinner than the bulk membrane thickness (30 Å), regardless of scrambling activity.
source: all the TMEM16 structures included in this study thin the membrane to 23 Å or less, which is at least 7 Å thinner than the bulk membrane thickness (30 Å), regardless of scrambling activity (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–5)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data shown in Figure 3A and supplements.

claim: Negligible scrambling activity (0–1 events in the groove) was observed in grooves that fail to thin the membrane to less than 14 Å and at the same time do not or very rarely sample TM4-TM6 distances above 6 Å.
source: We observed negligible scrambling activity (0–1 events in the groove) in grooves that fail to thin the membrane to less than 14 Å and at the same time do not or very rarely sample TM4-TM6 distances above 6 Å (Figure 3A, upper left quadrant)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All active scramblers have a minimal bilayer thickness below 14 Å.
source: all active scramblers have a minimal bilayer thickness below 14 Å
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data.

claim: The highest scrambling rates were observed in grooves that remain open, with TM4–TM6 distances above 6 Å, throughout most of the simulation.
source: we observed the highest scrambling rates in grooves that remain open, with TM4–TM6 distances above 6 Å, throughout most of the simulation (shaded region)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of the dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed <14 Å membrane thickness.
source: we want to clarify that lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of the dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed <14 Å membrane thickness (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The major determinant of lipid scrambling by TMEM16s is dilation of the TM4/TM6 groove.
source: Thus, the major determinant of lipid scrambling by TMEM16s is dilation of the TM4/TM6 groove
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation data analysis.

claim: Hydrophobic residues (H/F518, W619, and M522) at the midpoint of the TMEM16F pathway dynamically swing open to sporadically allow lipids through.
source: we noticed that hydrophobic residues (H/F518, W619, and M522) at the midpoint of the pathway, previously identified as an activation gate (Le et al., 2019b), dynamically swing open to sporadically allow lipids through (Figure 3—figure supplement 6C; Figure 3—videos 3 and 5)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6C and videos.

claim: The WT open TMEM16F structure (6QP6*) has half the single subunit scrambling rate compared to the F518H mutant.
source: the WT open structure (6QP6*) has half the single subunit scrambling rate
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative results from the simulation data.

claim: The TMEM16K subunit with more scrambling activity (eight times more) spent more time in an open-groove configuration.
source: we observed that the subunit with more scrambling activity (eight times more) spent more time in an open-groove configuration (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.

claim: Scrambling occurs more frequently when the groove is open for TMEM16K and F.
source: Qualitatively, scrambling occurs more frequently when the groove is open for TMEM16K and F (black dots in Figure 3B)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The consistently open Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 structure (PDB ID 4WIS) allows lipid headgroups to scramble in an uninterrupted fashion.
source: the consistently open Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 structure (PDB ID 4WIS) allows lipid headgroups to scramble in an uninterrupted fashion (Figure 3B, Figure 3—video 1)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Figure 3B and video 1.

claim: Two scrambling events were observed for a predicted ion-conductive TMEM16A state (5OYB*) which samples an average TM4–TM6 distance very close to the 6 Å threshold for scrambling.
source: we did observe two events for a predicted ion-conductive state (5OYB*) which samples an average TM4–TM6 distance very close, but just below, to the empirically determined 6 Å threshold for scrambling (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is a result from the simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The flow of lipid in TMEM16A is obstructed by residues at the center of the groove (I550, I551, and K645), and they more rarely separate to allow lipids to pass.
source: the flow of lipid is obstructed by residues at the center of the groove (I550, I551, and K645), and in TMEM16A they more rarely separate to allow lipids to pass (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.

claim: Lipids in TMEM16A are notably more stagnant in the pore than in the open TMEM16Fs and appear to be stabilized by electrostatic interactions with two charged residues, E633 and K645.
source: Lipids are also notably more stagnant in the pore than in the open TMEM16Fs and appear to be stabilized by electrostatic interactions with two charged residues, E633 and K645 (Figure 3—video 4)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Figure 3—video 4.

claim: Scrambling occurs in an identical manner across the TMEM16 family.
source: Despite these individual differences in groove dynamics, scrambling occurs in an identical manner across the family
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing simulation data across family members.

claim: Scrambling lipids move through the TM4/TM6 groove quickly, with dwell times for individual lipids below 20 ns.
source: Scrambling lipids move through the TM4/TM6 groove quickly, with dwell times for individual lipids below 20 ns
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data.

claim: Longer dwell times were observed for TMEM16K and TMEM16F at the groove constriction points, whereas in other scramblases, the dwell times are more evenly distributed along the groove.
source: However, we observed longer dwell times for TMEM16K and TMEM16F at the groove constriction points, whereas in other scramblases, the dwell times are more evenly distributed along the groove (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Among the scramblases, the free energy profile for lipids moving through the open groove is barrierless (<1 kT).
source: Among the scramblases, the free energy profile for lipids moving through the open groove is barrierless (<1 kT) (Appendix 1—figure 3A)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3A.

claim: The mean diffusion coefficient for lipids in the groove is between 10 and 16 Å2/ns among the scramblase homologs.
source: with similar kinetics among the homologs and a mean diffusion coefficient between 10 and 16 Å2/ns (Appendix 1—figure 4)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Scrambling events enter and leave the groove at random locations with only 3–10% of events passing through the high-density lipid regions on lower TM4 and upper TM6/TM8.
source: Scrambling events also enter and leave the groove at random locations (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5) with only 3–10% of events passing through the high-density lipid regions on lower TM4 and upper TM6/TM8 (Figure 1B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) at the intracellular and extracellular entrances of the nhTMEM16 groove were previously hypothesized to help organize or stabilize scrambling lipids.
source: We previously identified four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) at the intracellular and extracellular entrances of the nhTMEM16 groove that we hypothesized help organize or stabilize scrambling lipids (Bethel and Grabe, 2016; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: This is a reference to a prior hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: Although the four residues at the nhTMEM16 groove entrances have elevated contact frequencies, more than half of the contacts are made with bulk lipids that never scramble.
source: However, our CGMD of the same nhTMEM16 structure shows that although these residues have elevated contact frequencies, more than half of the contacts are made with bulk lipids that never scramble (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The in-the-groove scrambling events were Poisson distributed for all open and transiently open scramblases.
source: the in-the-groove scrambling events were Poisson distributed for all open and transiently open scramblases (Appendix 1—figure 5)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: Lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion.
source: indicating lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Poisson distribution of scrambling events.

claim: Permeation through the closed scramblase structures was low, <30 events per μs on average.
source: As expected, permeation through the closed scramblase structures was low, <30 events per μs on average
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data.

claim: Dilated TM4/TM6 grooves support 300–550 water permeation events per μs on average.
source: while dilated TM4/TM6 grooves (five out of six Ca2+-bound) support 300–550 permeation events per μs on average
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data.

claim: Even when the groove is inaccessible to lipids in closed and intermediate states, including the TMEM16A ion channel path, it remains hydrated with the waters shielded from the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
source: even when the groove is inaccessible to lipids in closed and intermediate states, including the TMEM16A ion channel path, it remains hydrated with the waters shielded from the hydrophobic core of the membrane (Appendix 1—figure 2A, closed)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2A.

claim: In open grooves, the water is exposed to the membrane core and lipid headgroups occupy the fully hydrated groove to bridge the leaflets.
source: in open grooves, the water is exposed to the membrane core and lipid headgroups occupy the fully hydrated groove to bridge the leaflets (Appendix 1—figure 2A, open)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2A.

claim: Spontaneous permeation of Na+ and Cl− ions through the scramblase TMEM16 grooves and TMEM16A pore was observed.
source: We also observed spontaneous permeation of Na+ and Cl− ions through the scramblase TMEM16 grooves and TMEM16A pore (Appendix 1—figure 2B; number of permeation events in Source data 1)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2B.

claim: Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) showed highest ion conductance followed by Ca2+-free nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), which was 3 times lower, and then Ca2+-bound afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), which was another three times lower again.
source: Of the fungal structures, only the scrambling-competent open states sampled multiple ion permeation events with Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) showing highest conductance followed by Ca2+-free nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), which was 3 times lower, and then Ca2+-bound afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), which was another three times lower again
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the simulation data.

claim: Cation-to-anion selectivity ratios of 5.1, 3.2, and 6 were measured for Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16, Ca2+-free nhTMEM16, and Ca2+-bound afTMEM16, respectively.
source: We also measured cation-to-anion selectivity ratios of 5.1, 3.2, and 6 for each simulation, respectively, computed from the ratio of total counts (PNa/PCl)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulation data.

claim: Both fungal scramblases transport anions and cations and both are weakly cation selective according to experiments.
